In [[mathematical analysis]], the '''dyadic derivative''' is a concept that extends the notion of [[derivative|classical differentiation]] to functions defined on the [[dyadic group]] or the dyadic field. Unlike classical differentiation, which is based on the [[limit (mathematics)|limit]] of difference quotients, dyadic differentiation is defined using dyadic (binary) addition and reflects the discontinuous nature of [[Walsh function]]s.

== Definition ==
=== Pointwise dyadic derivative ===
For a function <math>f</math> defined on [0,1), the first ''pointwise dyadic derivative'' of <math>f</math> at a point <math>x</math> is defined as:
:<math>f^{[1]}(x) = \lim_{m \to \infty} \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} 2^{j-1}[f(x) - f(x \oplus 2^{-j-1})]</math>

if this limit exists. Here, <math>\oplus</math> denotes the dyadic addition operation, which is defined using the [[binary representation|dyadic (binary) representation]] of numbers.<ref name="Engels-1985"/> That is, if
:<math>x = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} x_j 2^{-j-1}</math> and <math>y = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} y_j 2^{-j-1}</math> with <math>x_j, y_j \in \{0, 1\}</math>,
then
:<math>x \oplus y = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} (x_j \oplus y_j) 2^{-j-1}</math>,
where
:<math>x_j \oplus y_j = (x_j + y_j) \pmod 2</math>.<ref name="Engels-1985"/><ref name="Onneweer-1979"/>

Higher-order dyadic derivatives are defined [[recursion (mathematics)|recursively]]: <math>f^{[r]}(x) = (f^{[r-1]})^{[1]}(x)</math> for <math>r \in \mathbb N</math>.<ref name="Engels-1985"/>

=== Strong dyadic derivative ===

The ''strong dyadic derivative'' is defined in the context of [[function space]]s. Let <math>X(0, 1)</math> denote one of the function spaces <math>L^p(0, 1)</math> for <math>1 \le p \le \infty</math> ([[Lp_space|''L''<sup>''p''</sup> space]]); <math>L^\infty(0, 1)</math> ([[L-infinity|''L''<sup>''∞''</sup> space]]); or <math>C^\oplus[0, 1]</math> (the space of dyadically continuous functions). If <math>f \in X(0, 1)</math> and there exists <math>g \in X(0, 1)</math> such that
:<math>\lim_{m \to \infty} \left\| \sum_{j=0}^{m-1} 2^{j-1}[f(\cdot) - f(\cdot \oplus 2^{-j-1})] - g(\cdot) \right\|_X = 0</math>,
then <math>g</math> is called the first strong dyadic derivative of <math>f</math>, denoted by <math>g = D^{[1]}f</math>.<ref name="Engels-1985">Engels, W. (1985). "On the characterization of the dyadic derivative". ''[[Acta Mathematica Hungarica]]'', 46(1-2): 47-56.</ref> Higher-order derivatives can be defined recursively similar to pointwise dyadic derivatives.

== Properties ==
Similar to the classic derivative in calculus, the dyadic derivative possesses several properties.

=== Linearity ===
The dyadic derivative is a [[linear operator]]. If functions <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are dyadically differentiable and <math>\alpha, \beta</math> are [[Mathematical constant|constant]]s, then <math>\alpha f + \beta g</math> is dyadically differentiable:
:<math>(\alpha f + \beta g)^{[1]} = \alpha f^{[1]} + \beta g^{[1]}</math>.<ref name="Butzer-1973">Butzer, P. L., and Wagner, H. J. (1973). "Walsh-Fourier series and the concept of a derivative". ''Applicable Analysis'', 3(1): 29-46.</ref>

=== Closure ===
The dyadic differentiation operator is closed; that is, if <math>f</math> is in the [[domain of a function|domain]] of the [[Operator (mathematics)|operator]], then its dyadic derivative also belongs to the same function space.<ref name="Onneweer-1979">Onneweer, C.W. (1979). "On the definition of dyadic differentiation". ''Applicable Analysis'', 9(4): 267-278.</ref>

=== Inverse operator ===
There exists a dyadic [[Integral linear operator|integration operator]] that serves as an [[inverse operator|inverse]] to the dyadic differentiation operator, analogous to the [[fundamental theorem of calculus]].<ref>Schipp, F. (1976). "Über gewisse Maximaloperatoren". ''Annales Univ. Sci. Budapestinensis de Rolando Eötvös Nominatae, Sec. Math.'', 28: 145-152.</ref>

=== Relationship to the Walsh-Fourier transform ===
For functions <math>f</math> where <math>D^{[1]}f \in L_1(G)</math> exists, the [[Walsh-Fourier transform]] satisfies:
:<math>[D^{[1]}f]^{\wedge}(\chi) = |\chi|\hat{f}(\chi)</math>
for all [[Character (mathematics)|characters]] <math>\chi</math>, where <math>|\chi|</math> represents the [[norm (mathematics)|norm]] of the character.<ref name="Onneweer-1977">Onneweer, C. W. (1977). "Fractional differentiation on the group of integers of a p-adic or p-series field". ''Analysis Mathematica'', 3(2): 119-130.</ref>

=== Eigenfunctions ===
The Walsh functions <math>\psi_k</math> are [[eigenfunction]]s of the dyadic differentiation operator with corresponding eigenvalues related to their index:
:<math>D^{[1]}\psi_k = \psi_k^{[1]} = k\psi_k</math>
and
:<math>D^{[r]}\psi_k = \psi_k^{[r]} = k^r \psi_k</math>.
This eigenfunction property makes Walsh functions naturally suited for analysis involving dyadic derivatives, similar to how [[complex exponential]]s <math>e^{ikx}</math> are eigenfunctions of classical differentiation.<ref name="Engels-1985"/>

=== Characterization of differentiable functions ===
Thanks to a generalization of a result of Butzer and Wagner,<ref name="Engels-1985"/>
<blockquote>
'''Theorem (Skvorcov—Wade).''' Let <math>f</math> be continuous on <math>[0, 1)</math>, and let <math>f^{[1]}</math> exist for all but countably many
points <math>x \in (0, 1)</math>. Then <math>f</math> is [[constant function|constant]].<ref>V. A. Skvorcov, W. R. Wade (1979). "Generalizations of some results concerning Walsh series and the dyadic derivative". ''Analysis Mathematica'', 5, 249-255.</ref>
</blockquote>
This result implies that it is more interesting to consider functions that are ''not'' continuous over the entire interval. A generalization of the above result shows that:
<blockquote>
'''Theorem.''' A [[bounded function]] defined on <math>[0,1)</math> with a [[countable set]] of [[discontinuity (mathematics)|discontinuities]] (exclusively of [[jump discontinuities]]) that have at most a finite number of cluster points is pointwise dyadically differentiable ''except'' on a countable set if and only if it is a [[step function|piecewise constant function]].<ref name="Engels-1985" />
</blockquote>

== Examples ==

{| class="wikitable"
! Function type !! Example !! Dyadic derivative !! Notes
|-
| [[Constant function]]s || <math>f(x) = C</math> for all <math>x \in [0,1)</math> || <math>f^{[1]}(x) = 0</math> || Similar to classical calculus<ref name="Engels-1985"/>
|-
| [[Step function]]s || <math>g(x) = \begin{cases}
3, & x \in [0,1/4) \\
-1, & x \in [1/4,1)
\end{cases}</math> || <math>g^{[1]}(x) = \begin{cases}
6, & x \in [0,1/4) \\
-4, & x \in [1/4,1/2) \\
-2, & x \in [1/2,3/4) \\
0, & x \in [3/4,1)
\end{cases}</math> || Creates additional [[discontinuity (mathematics)|discontinuities]]<ref name="Engels-1985"/>
|-
| [[Dirichlet function]] || <math>d(x) = \begin{cases}
1, & x \in [0,1) \cap \mathbb{Q} \\
0, & x \in [0,1) \setminus \mathbb{Q}
\end{cases}</math> || <math>d^{[1]}(x) = 0</math> for all <math>x \in [0,1)</math> || Differentiable despite [[dense set|dense]] discontinuities<ref name="Engels-1985"/>
|-
| [[Walsh function]]s || <math>\psi_k(x)</math> || <math>\psi_k^{[1]}(x) = k\psi_k(x)</math> || [[Eigenfunction]]s of the dyadic derivative<ref name="Butzer-1973"/>
|-
| [[Linear function]]s || <math>f(x) = x</math> || Not dyadic differentiable || Contrasts with classical calculus<ref name="Engels-1985"/>
|}

== History ==
The dyadic derivative was introduced by mathematician James Edmund Gibbs in the context of [[Walsh function]]s and further developed by [[Paul Butzer]] and Heinz-Joseph Wagner.<ref>Gibbs, J. E., and Ireland, B. (1974). "Walsh functions and differentiation". ''Proceedings of the Symposium and Workshop on Applications of Walsh-Functions''. Naval Research Laboratory, Washington, D.C., pp. 1-29.</ref><ref name="Butzer-1973">Butzer, P. L., and Wagner, H. J. (1973). "Walsh-Fourier series and the concept of a derivative". ''Applicable Analysis'', 3(1): 29-46.</ref> 

Further contributions came from C. W. Onneweer, who extended the concept to [[fractional differentiation]] and [[p-adic|''p''-adic]] fields.<ref name="Onneweer-1977"/> In 1979, Onneweer provided alternative definitions to the dyadic derivatives.<ref name="Onneweer-1979"/>
